title: Raw loop passback: Ryan Goh
content:
Candidate: Ryan Goh (applied for Senior Runtime Engineer - Serving Runtime)
Loop date: 2024-05-09 (remote)
Interviewer mix: Marcus (systems/SLOs), Evelyn (kernel/quant), Sophie (org fit + comp/ops)
Stage: On-site / loop phase
Top-line quick notes (raw):
- Smart, pragmatic engineer. Strong familiarity with low-level perf tuning (CUDA kernels, memory layout) but hesitant on distributed autoscaling trade-offs.
- Communicates clearly; writes concise diagrams on whiteboard.
- Some gaps in product trade-off framing for multi-tenant inference (cost vs latency routing).
- Compensation expectation: asked about mid-Senior band; flagged to comp team.

Detailed scratch notes (by interviewer):
- Marcus (systems / SLOs): 10:05-10:35
  - System-design prompt: design a multi-tenant model serving mesh with predictable p95 latency under bursty load.
  - Ryan sketched a tiered routing approach: hot-path pinned model replicas + cold-path on-demand scaled pods. Good callouts on KV cache usage to reduce cold-start tokens.
  - Missed quantization-aware scheduling: didn't initially consider model-variant matching when routing by latency/cost; needed prompting to mention fallback to quantized variants.
  - SRE-ish questions: rollout and canary -> proposed gradual traffic shift + shadowing. Lacked concrete metrics to monitor (suggested CPU/GPU util but not queue wait time).
  - Note: he mentioned prior experience with Node-level GPU isolation (NVIDIA MIG) and had an anecdote about a 30% tail latency reduction after rebalancing collocated workloads. Credible and specific numbers.

- Evelyn (kernels / inference perf): 11:00-11:40
  - Deep dive into attention kernel optimizations and KV cache strategy. Ryan could reason about blocking vs. streaming attention and tradeoffs for long-sequence costs.
  - Good mental model for quantized GEMM path; however, when pressed about correctness vs. perf for int8 quantization he deferred to "model teams" for calibration steps (we want eng candidates who can at least outline calibration).
  - Code question (small pseudo-code): find and fix a memory leak scenario in a simplified GPU buffer lifecycle. He found the leak quickly and suggested an RAII-style ownership pattern. Strong debugging instincts.
  - Red flag?: did not volunteer experience with Triton/TVM; had worked more with PyTorch/XLA stacks. Not a dealbreaker but needs ramp for our runtime toolchain.

- Sophie (org fit / ownership): 12:10-12:30
  - Behavioral: told story about owning a cross-team rollout to upgrade model shards; highlighted stakeholder management and prioritization. Solid PM-sense.
  - On tradeoffs: tended to default to "opt for simplicity and iterate" which aligns with our philosophy, but when pushed about long-term operating costs, wanted more quantitative estimates.
  - Culture fit: collaborative, asked good clarifying Qs, seemed energized by shipping and reducing unit cost.

Strengths (bullet):
- Low-level performance debugging and memory management (concrete examples).
- Clear communicator and good at cross-team coordination.
- Pragmatic approach on shipping and observability hooks.

Weaknesses / Concerns:
- Less experience with our runtime stack (Triton, TVM) and some orchestration/autoscaling design corners (node-level scheduling when GPUs are heterogenous).
- Less ownership on quantization calibration pipeline (mostly relied on model teams in prior role).
- Product framing on cost-vs-latency could be stronger (we need engineers who can push back and quantify options).

Scorecard (raw, 1-5):
- Technical depth (algorithms/kernel): 4/5
- Systems design (multi-tenant, routing): 3/5
- Debugging (triage & fix): 5/5
- Communication & collaboration: 4/5
- Product sense / cost-awareness: 3/5
- Overall (avg): 3.8/5 -> rounded to 3.5/5 for loop notes

Interviewers' raw recommendation: hold/second-stage follow-up. Not an immediate yes because of runtime-tooling gaps but strong candidate if we can pair him with onboarding + short ramp program.

Questions / follow-ups we should ask candidate (if moving forward):
- Walk us through a concrete quantization calibration you were part of: steps, metrics you measured, how you validated quality loss.
- How would you design a scheduling policy for mixed-precision GPUs (A100+T4) to minimize cost while meeting p95 targets? Ask for specific metrics and reaction to spike scenarios.
- Which pieces of Triton/TVM would you expect to change to support rapid model rollouts?
- Compensation: can he be specific on current comp and expected target? (He gave a band; need exact numbers).

Action items (for Sophie):
- TODO: ask comp team for target band match (ENG-SR-2) and whether interviewer's comp expectation lines up.
- TODO: schedule a short follow-up with one engineer from our Triton/quant team (30m) to test familiarity and ramp plan. Suggested interviewer: Priya or Marcus follow-up.
- TODO: request reference specifically on calibration/quantization pipeline (prior manager who owns model quality).

Notes to self (stream-of-consciousness):
- Candidate would probably ramp quickly on our infra; fits culture and shipping mentality.
- If we can pair him with a 2-4 week focused onboarding on "model-variant rollouts + Triton basics" he could be a net win.
- Consider a conditional offer with a 3-month success plan tied to ownership of a caching/batching optimization.

Potential blockers for hire committee:
- Does the comp band align? (ask comp)
- Are we comfortable with the runtime-tooling ramp? (engineering agrees to pairing/mentorship)

Misc scribbles (untidy):
- "memory leak fix -> RAII pattern" (good example for take-home)
- "30% tail reduction anecdote" (ask for numbers/PR or perf dashboard link in references)
- Slack thread where candidate posted an explanation of quantization (linked above)

Verdict summary (one-liner for panel):
Well-rounded senior with strong debugging and low-level skills, moderate systems-design gaps specific to our stack — recommend a targeted follow-up interview and comp check before advancing to onsite offer conversation.

End of raw passback.
